posts.text: You can also read the README from Lego Blockly Github (link provided in the first post, here it is: https://github.com/BlissCA/lego-blockly/blob/dev/README.md You will then find this in the supported devices: VLL : Virtal Light Link for Code Pilot and MicroScout brick. Using an USB-Serial FTDI adapter and a Led + Resistor connected to DTR Pin and GND (or +3.3V depending) OR you can use the RCX USB Tower which has VLL capabilities. (Category RCX/CM in Lego Blockly) @Toasties made a table in the previous thread but would need some updates already... I already thought of the IDEA of a table or list but did not yet do something... Meanwhile, I try to maintain the Github README up to date. So for your MicroScout (in 9748 set), which uses VLL, the easiest is to use the RCX USB Tower (NOT CM) (Lego Blockly Category RCX/CM -> VLL in the toolbox). If you don't have the USB Tower, then, an FTDI with a LED (I use White LED) and a resistor will do the trick, (Category VLL Serial for the FTDI solution).

posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: I doubt it is that it is too expensive to make it profitable but more that there is not the market to make it worthwhile or profitable no matter what the cost is. 9V has been gone 15 years, to expect a company to keep making adapters as they change their products is unrealistic. They are also simple electronics and enthusiastic fans (especially fans of vintage items that are used to repairing) will typically make them, and so LEGO probably knows that even if they made a 9V-PUp converter (and a separate PF converter and a separate 12V converter), then fans would still make their own cheaper bespoke versions that do exactly what they want them to do. It is understandable that LEGO wants all of the electronic products that are available at one time are compatible but not necessarily compatible with products with those from over a decade before. What I'd prefer to see is a guarantee from LEGO that they will support a system until a specific date, so that you will always be able to buy components for that system until that date and if a new system is introduced in that time then compatability adapters will be available. That way, a buyer knows that their (probably expensive) product will have official support and compatability for a given time and may well put off investing in items if close to the end or buy plenty of spares if they are nearing the end of support date. A lot of my kit is PF and although I bought plenty of spare official motors when they were nearing the end, the extension cables sold out quickly and weren’t restocked. If I had known that, I would probably have bought more for cutting and modifying. Even used connectors are getting expensive now that I tend to attach small banana plugs to official connectors rather than hard wiring a motor to a connector, so I can easily swap out the (unofficial) motor if I want to change it. I also find now buying old IR receivers can be cheaper than official connectors!

posts.title: Bounty Boat, Lego 6247: A Fresh Review
posts.text: In the decades following Lego's release of the original pirate wave of 1989, building techniques have evolved. Color palette and piece inventory has evolved. Designs have become significantly more elaborate. And it would appear, for the most part, that these changes have been welcomed by the vast majority of consumers. But what about those of us who are overly nostalgic (read: "stuck in the past") about vintage sets? What venue do you have if you are more inclined toward the vintage "play sets" more than the modern "display sets?" If that description resonates with you, then this "Fresh Review" series* is for you! The purpose of this series is to bring a fresh look to older, vintage sets. Specifically their ability to be adapted and reimagined into other (albeit similar) sets. Since the history of vintage Lego Pirates is readily available to all of us, and really cannot be recreated or improved upon, these posts will focus on my own impressions and solicit similar impressions from those of you who read and feel inclined to comment. This post will focus on 1992's "Bounty Boat." When you look at the original box art it's actually kind of mind blowing what you were getting for $4.25 even back in 1992. A very specialized piece in the rowboat itself combined with 3 minifigures? A treasure chest with "gold" and tools to either dig it up or bury it? That's an epic value for a set that topped out at 36 pieces. And if you were 12 years old in 1992 (I was) this set was an accessible entry into the new wave of pirate sets Lego offered that year. The pirates themselves hadn't changed much. They were still up to their old pillaging and plundering ways. But the "good guys" were completely new, even though they were basically just recoloring of the original blue coats. By 1992 I had a few blue coat sets, like Harbor Sentry, Sabre Island, and Lagoon Lockup. I also had the Pirates Minigfigures set from 1989, a precursor to today's "battle pack." But when I saw Lego recolor the bluecoats into redcoats, I knew I had to have both. Bounty Boat was my fastest ticket to achieve this. So let's take a look at this relatively simple set, shall we? Like I said, this set itself is actually pretty simple. It features a rowboat (still pretty new and exciting by 1992 standards) and 3 minifigs, all of which were recolored versions of their predecessors. Getting a treasure chest, some chrome gold coins, and some tools and weapons just round out the package made it all even better. The set itself is excellent value for the 1992 money: Two Imperial Guards recovering some plundered treasure from a captured scalawag, who they've forced into service by making him row the boat, dig up the treasure, and so on. For a small set to include both pirates and imperials is remarkable. The 1989 wave didn't really have any smaller sets that included members of both the pirates and imperial factions aside from Lego 6251. In order to get a member of both factions you had to get either Eldorado Fortress or Forbidden Island. Lego did somewhat address this in 1991 with Lagoon Lockup and Broadside's Brig both of which were mid-sized sets. That year they also included both factions in Rock Island Refuge. The thing is, we've got to consider what $10 USD represented to a lower middle class child at that time. That's a lot of lawns mowed and driveways snow-shoveled. That's a lot of firewood stacked, allowances saved (if your home was fortunate enough that your parents could give you an allowance) and, if I'm being honest, dreams crushed. Even Broadside's Brig opened at just under $9 USD. Lagoon Lockup was closer to $30 and Rock Island Refuge was an intangible $65+ USD. So imagine my excitement when I discovered, first, an all new (albeit recolored) faction from Lego and second, at the amazing price of $4.25 USD! posts.title: Marvel Superheroes 2026 - Rumors & Discussion
posts.text: Thumbs up on the skyline. With all the references and inclusions from across comics, it feels like a labour of love from a true believer. The scaling of some of the mini-ships is laughable—and with the Quinjet or Leviathan, the builds are pretty lacking that I'd just as soon remove them. A minifig Galactus feels absolutely unreal to see and is undoubtedly the highlight of this set. To be honest, I have no interest in this set besides him—and I imagine a lot of the secondary market would feel the same—so I'd like to see him in another set down the road; an Easter egg in a Baxter Building or "Icons of Marvel Comics," maybe? Seems like a great mix between the Architecture and Marvel crowds. I'm glad this concept wasn't split up into five GwPs or collector sets, ala the $40 Disneyland sets—while that'd make it an easier buy for me since all I really want is the minifig, it'd feel especially repetitive to start a new line after two scales of Marvel modulars in the past couple years. Including it all in one package keeps it focused, and hopefully opens the door to, say, a microscale Asgard? (I say this as the Aslume-appointed Thunder Lord, of course.) I wish we could see something like this in LSW. I've already invested into the $300+-a-pop-modular line (as in I own only the '21 Daily Bugle), so all I can do is appreciate this from afar. That said, I like what I see, and if I ever see it on a deep discount, I'll likely buy just for the figs. I don't get any hope for future sets from this, given the sum whole is usually more popular than the parts individually. The purpose for including the niche locations was to fill out the skyline, which typically is not just two large skyscrapers and two short buildings like we've seen in the D2C line. In the latter's case, you could theoretically buy just one and call it done. (I won't because I'm a madman masquerading as a sword online, but I digress.) Thus the sets have to hold their own weight on factors beyond merely "this showed up in a recent project," or "this would feature a fanfavourite character;" it has to look visually appealing as a display piece, have it's own enduring iconicity, and (I think secondarily) feature a broad cast of beloved characters. For this reason I think an Oscorp (with Kaine, Daredevil, Luna Snow and Moon Knight) is the only way to go.

posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: Hi @Berthil, thanks for pointing that out! I have updated the link, hopefully it works correctly for you now. You’re right, there are several clock designs that use Technic Curved Gear Racks 11 x 11 (Part 24121) as a frame for the dial, and some, like yours, even use them to drive one of the hands. Yours is truly a beautiful clock, and from what I can see, it carries a remarkable level of mechanical complexity. Huge congratulations on such an extraordinary build! However, I believe my starting concept is quite different from yours. My clock was meant to be an abstract design concept, highlighting the complete absence of a traditional dial and a physical central axis. Making concentric rings rotate smoothly on their own without a real physical pivot presented its own unique set of challenges (certainly different from yours, but very interesting nonetheless!). If the link works for you now, you can check out the Creator Updates section on LEGO Ideas, where I shared a 3D breakdown of the model and the story behind some of the hurdles I encountered and solved. Using a motor was definitely a simpler choice compared to a pendulum or weight-driven system. But I designed this clock for myself as a functional, everyday object. A fully mechanical escapement system, as fascinating as it is, requires constant management and adjustments that I preferred to avoid. Sometimes simple solutions work best, especially when they don't compromise the core design. Thanks again for taking the time to share your thoughts, and I’d love to hear more of your feedback as the discussion evolves!

With TLG though I'd say it is even worse: They deliberately create new standards either without any backward compatibility or not providing any conversion "items" - in the simplest case, cables - altough otherwise feasible. Yes I know: There was a time when they did that: 9V-PF. 9V-NXT/EV3. And sure, with some tricks you could kill the electronics. But then: Who actually tried? 4.5V, 9V: 2 wires. PF: 4 wires. NXT/EV3: 6 wires. PUp 6 wires. All different plugs. Necessary? Yes sure. Conversion possible? Yes, sure, the electronics inside an NXT upward can >surely< sense what is attached. And back then, TLG made some ... Today, that is history. PUp hubs can control 9V and PF motors. There are no rotation encoders inside these motors, but the PUp protocol is well-prepared for that. Of course, it is. Nowadays, it is so super simple to make such things. The train folks know all about it; stone old classic 9V train motors run nicely on a PUp hub. Any PUp hub. Is there a 9V-PUp conversion cable? No. I bet because it is too expensive to make it profitable. Only for a couple of weird 9V freaks. New customers may not have heard about 9V at all. I get all that. It is so frustrating. The Chinese of course make them. Good that we have an Alt.Brand forum, so people can learn about it. Take TLG's 10V DC power supply for recharging the PF LiPo 8878 as another example. They sold that power supply for +€30! I have a thread on EB about that LiPo: It charges from 9V DC to 18V DC without >any< problems. But no, TLG came up with a 10V DC power supply. "Nobody" uses 10V DC ... why should they.
